blocks.text: Apocalyptic writing took shape among communities facing pressure, exile, and persecution as they asked how God would act. Its beasts, numbers, and cosmic scenes were familiar ways of speaking about empires and divine sovereignty, so Revelation’s imagery communicates through a symbolic mode rather than ordinary description alone.

Ancient empires used deportation and resettlement to control conquered peoples. Scripture treats exile as more than displacement: it involves covenant judgment, loss of land and temple, and testing of identity, while preserving hope for a remnant. Second Temple Jewish communities still knew partial return and diaspora life and hoped for fuller restoration. Jerusalem itself had moved from Jebusite city to Davidic capital and temple center, then became a focus of exile, return, and messianic expectation. New Jerusalem therefore appears as the biblical story’s final hope after judgment and exile, turning temple loss toward final dwelling and restored holiness.

Biblical creation texts stand alongside Mesopotamian origin traditions such as Enuma Elish and Atrahasis, but present creation as the ordered work of one covenant Lord. Creation is good and accountable to God, and humanity receives dignity and responsibility within it. Second Temple Jewish and early Christian writings often connected creation, wisdom, resurrection hope, and God’s power to make all things new, providing a broad setting for the opening vision of a new heaven and earth.

In cultures where death was usually treated as final, resurrection hope made a striking claim about God’s power and faithfulness. It affirmed both divine power over death and the renewal of God’s people. Bodily resurrection was debated within Second Temple Judaism, so the New Testament proclamation was rooted in an existing hope while also remaining disruptive. This background sharpens the force of the promise that death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.

Ancient temples were understood as divine dwellings and royal-cultic centers. Israel’s temple symbolism, however, was governed by covenant holiness and the Lord’s chosen presence, joining sacred space with sacrifice, priesthood, purity, and consecrated access. In the Second Temple period, the Jerusalem temple shaped pilgrimage, worship, national hope, and disputes over authority. That background gives particular weight to the vision’s surprising declaration that the city has no temple building because God and the Lamb are its temple.

sections.title: Temple and Presence Across the Story

blocks.text: The temple theme follows a long sequence: God’s tabernacle presence in the wilderness, Solomon’s temple in Jerusalem, the temple’s judgment and destruction, restored worship in the Second Temple, and Jesus’ identification of himself with temple fulfillment. Revelation 21 carries that sequence to New Jerusalem, where no separate temple is present because God and the Lamb dwell there.

One way to understand the ending is to notice how it holds cosmic and communal images together. It presents a new heaven and earth, New Jerusalem descending from God, God dwelling with humanity, and the end of death and mourning. It also portrays nations walking by the city’s light and earthly kings bringing their glory into it. Read together, these images suggest a final hope expressed at the scale of both the created world and life among peoples.

Sanctuary passages share the language of dwelling and holiness, but their referents must not be flattened into one: tabernacle, First and Second Temples, Christological and community metaphors, heavenly sanctuary, and new creation remain distinct. Keeping those distinctions also rules out using later Christian sanctuary interpretations to justify antisemitism, replacement claims, destruction or seizure of holy places, or institutional immunity from ethical accountability.

The city vision continues into Revelation 22:1-5. Across this larger passage, New Jerusalem combines city, bride, sanctuary, Eden, and renewed-Zion imagery. Revelation repeatedly reworks Israel’s Scriptures, especially Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Exodus, Zechariah, Genesis, and Psalms. Its sequence particularly recomposes Ezekielian images of the throne, scroll, measuring, battle, city, river, and tree.
